answer:
Dear SaaStr:  I’m trying to sell my 8-person start-up into large enterprises, but they just don’t want to talk with me …
The thing is, they do want to buy from startups and smaller vendors.  They are just very careful how much risk they take on any given vendor.   Especially if it’s not Fintech.
You have to earn their trust.  First by being able to deliver a real working pilot for free.  And second by earning your place as part of the ecosystem.
Most startups just aren’t willing or capable of doing this.  It requires more than half the team to be dedicated full-time to enterprise sales and customer success.  Often, that means you can never hit product-market fit.
But if you are willing to put in the work, then at least try to understand the social contract here:
First, it helps if there’s something else the Big Guy already has bought before (or owns) from another vendor … that does similar things.
This creates what I call the “Social Contract”.  In essence, when you buy a new app from a startup like us, you’re buying on faith.  But if that vendor also works well enough to let them deploy it across all departments, teams, groups, etc. within the company … then you’ve earned some respect.
It makes the risk more palatable.  And so many companies will start to buy more seats and modules from you.
Second, most CIOs sort of already know which smaller players that run the whole company might work out.  So even though they may not be ready to go live today, they’ll often still meet.
So ask!  Be direct.  Do a demo, build a working proof-of-concept together.  Show up.  Follow up.  Don’t send over someone junior.  Ask for a meeting, again.  Again.  Until they agree.
And once you get one win under your belt, you’ll find it gets easier and easier.
Third, you need to show up at every industry event, conference, and dinner.  Especially if the CEO attends, too.  Just showing up at Dreamforce as a sponsor doesn’t count.  Not really.  You gotta show up, too.  As CEO.  As founder.  With customers.
If you can figure out how to do these three things, you’ll be surprised how many doors open.

So we're coming up on SaaStr Annual again, and I'm super excited for it this year because we've got some really incredible speakers lined up.
And I want to tell you just one story before we get going here today that's so important.
So I met with the head of IT at a Fortune 500 company not too long ago,
and he was incredibly smart.
I mean, when he was a kid, his dad took him to see IBM's first mainframe computers.
He went to Stanford as an undergrad, then did two graduate degrees there.
And now he runs IT at a big company.
But here's what's interesting.
This is the same person who said to me:
"I don't care if your product works or not, I don't even know how it does what it says.
What I do know is my job is to make sure everyone has Internet access."

I got nothing better to do right now than give all these people Internet access."

Not only would he never buy from them,
he wouldn't have time to meet with them either.
The reality is that the more senior you go in an enterprise, the less likely anyone is going to ask you to evaluate a new vendor unless it saves their butt.
Unless it makes them look like heroes.
They won't do it otherwise.
You need to understand the social contract between you and the buyers that matter most.

answer:
So one of our favorite SaaS leaders is Monday.com.  We were early investors back when it was called “Dapulse” and they were just getting going.
It’s an incredible story of bootstrapping to IPO, and building something that now has almost 200,000 customers across 190+ countries!
The numbers are pretty epic:
$600m run-rate (!)
Growing 29% year-over-year (or 24% adjusted for currency effects) — so still very much in growth mode.
Almost 90% gross margins,
And profitable!  They’ve been profitable for quite some time, even though most don’t see them as typical of a B2B leader today.
Pretty impressive.
Now let’s dig into some interesting learnings here:
#1.  76% of their revenue comes from outside North America
This isn’t unusual anymore, but it’s helpful to see how this plays out with a global leader like Monday.com.  The majority of its customers may be based in North America, but they pay globally.
#2.  85% NRR from SMBs.  But up to 100% NRR from larger customers
We often think of higher NRR being tied to bigger deals and more complex software, and indeed it can be.  But also, we know many SMB leaders have seen insane levels of NRR.  Asana and HubSpot both do.   Monday.com does too, albeit at a slightly lower level than these two leaders.  Its smallest customers are worth less on average, and churn out faster … so they have to work harder to keep them happy.
#3.  60% self-service / direct sales motion; 40% channel
A common split, but helpful to see.  A lot of Monday’s smaller customers buy directly through their website, but larger ones prefer working with partners.
#4.  35% of revenue from new logo customers each quarter
Another good benchmark.  You’d expect Monday to get a huge boost from upsells given its high net retention rates, but actually, only about half its growth comes from existing customers expanding their usage.  So yes, upsell matters at scale.  But new logos matter too.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: What Are Some Ways To Really Stand Out In A Job Interview?
First and foremost, be honest.
A mediocre candidate who is really good at interviewing often stands out.  But also … you’ll get caught eventually if it’s not you.
Second, bring great stories.
This is how you stand out.  The best candidates always have so many amazing stories to share.  So many.  Share them.  And make sure they are real, too.
Third, ask thoughtful questions ahead of time — and then come up with even more thoughtful ones during the interview itself:
Ask what the biggest challenges are for this role now, today, this week.  Ask why she or he wants to hire someone right now.  Get some answers back, ideally via email before the meeting.  Then show up knowing where to add value, right off the bat.
Fourth, understand their product cold
.  If you don’t know Salesforce, but want to work on a sales team?  You’re already behind.  Learn it.  Read all the materials here, watch YouTube videos, read every single question on Quora on that topic.
Fifth, do your homework on the company
.  Don’t just go through Crunchbase.  Do social media searches, etc.  This will help you identify the top problems facing the start-up and allow you to tailor your approach based on those needs.
Sixth, highlight something you’ve done well
.  Everyone knows how important follow-ups are.  Highlighting that you did three follow ups a day as an AE is great.  Even better though, if you can explain one way you got a customer to pay $10k+ ACV (or whatever) that another rep couldn’t.  That helps everyone see you might actually deliver results.
Seventh, don’t be afraid to talk about failures and mistakes
.  Especially if they were big enough that you learned a lot.

“Doubling Down” is a new series where we hear from top B2B SaaS investors on their most recent activities and takes on the current market. We had a great one last week with David Frankel, General Partner at Forerunner Ventures.
This week we’re focusing on Mark Roberge, Co-Founder and Managing Director at Stage 2 Capital!
#1. What’s your current activity focus?  (e.g., investing, board work, LP commitments)
Currently focused on portfolio development, company building and LP fundraising for our $150M Stage 2 Capital II fund, which will be deployed primarily into early stage software companies. I’m also maintaining strong relationships with my existing portfolio companies as they continue to scale through growth stages.
#2. Where are you seeing the biggest opportunities right now?
We believe that AI represents an enormous opportunity for software businesses. Many of these opportunities exist today but many more can emerge over time. As founders leverage these technologies, we should see a significant increase in efficiency gains and customer value creation across various categories.

There isn’t much keeping me awake lately other than thinking about how we can help our entrepreneurs build better products faster while creating sustainable long-term business models.
#4. What advice would you give to first-time SaaS founders raising capital?
I tell them all the same thing – hire someone good! Whether it’s a co-founder or employee, make sure you bring people onto your team who have expertise and complement your skills.
#5. How do you stay current with what’s happening in B2B / SaaS? What sources do you rely on?
Stage 2 Capital maintains strong connections with leading industry conferences such as Dreamforce, SaaStr Annual, Web Summit and Replit Festival. Additionally, I regularly read reports and articles published by influential research firms like Gartner, Bain and McKinsey, as well as news outlets such as Bloomberg Businessweek and TechCrunch.

So many folks are worried today that public multiples have fallen to crazy lows.
I mean — they have:
The average SaaS company is now trading at just 6x ARR.
That’s down from 17x back in Q1’22 and as low as 5x for software overall!
Now it may be even worse than you think.  If interest rates stay high, and growth stays relatively low, then these multiples could fall much further.
But … will it matter too much?
At least if you aren’t raising VC capital again right this minute (you probably won’t).
If you’re already profitable or close to it, growing nicely but not crazily, with happy customers … what does it really matter if your stock trades at say 5x-7x revenue instead of 15x?
It doesn’t change your business model
.  It doesn’t make things harder on you.  The public markets can be brutal and unforgiving, yes. But they don’t affect how much money your customers pay each month. They don’t affect how much you spend on sales & marketing. And they don’t effect your ability to raise prices when appropriate, etc. etc.
In fact, lower market caps often help.  Lower market cap means less dilution.
Lower market caps also usually mean less pressure to grow faster, hire more people, etc.  That’s good for everyone on the team.
So while having a higher market cap is always nice, I wouldn’t let fear creep into your mind around low market caps.
What matters most is
your
growth rate
. Not the market multiple. At least after Initial Traction.
You’ve likely heard this before, but I wanted to remind founders here, especially given all the noise out there around multiples being “too low”.  Don’t worry too much about it.  Just keep doing great things.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: How do you know if your company is an “NRR Zombie”?
I think we all can see them now.  Companies with high NRR … but not enough revenue from that base to really grow the business.
These are zombies because they aren’t growing, and it’s hard to imagine how they ever will without some radical change (acquisition), or massive increase in sales cycles, or something else dramatic.
And yet, many have such high NRR — often 120%+ — that at least on paper, you’d think there should be more growth here.
Sometimes, these companies get sold for a good price anyway. Sometimes, they just kind of stagnate, even as their customer count grows and churn falls.
Some examples:
ServiceNow was stuck this way until its $1B ARR, when it finally started to accelerate again
Salesforce itself took 10 years to hit 100% NRR
Zendesk has been stuck below 110%, though it got better in Q2’20
Atlassian struggled here, too,
until it crossed $500m ARR or so and had a few big customers push it over
So what can you do? First, don’t panic. Second, make sure your NRR isn’t going down. That would be worse than being a zombie. Third, focus energy on bigger deals to drive up ACV
. A lot of NRR Zombies end up focused almost exclusively on SMBs, which can create a ceiling on overall revenue. Fourth, find new ways to monetize existing customers
. More seats, more agents, more modules. Fifth, look at other leaders like Zoom who didn’t truly break out until well after $200m ARR. And sixth, make sure your churn isn’t hidden by upsells
. Some NRR Zombies have low churn, but hide it by upselling and adding new services.

Dear SaaStr: Our CFO Sounds Very Polished But We Are Missing The Burn Rate By Almost $1M A Month. What Can We Do?
It’s not really uncommon to see this. You want a polished, experienced CFO and you get one. They’ve been doing it for years, they know all the right things to say, they look great on LinkedIn.
But then when it comes time to roll up their sleeves and actually do real planning with your head of finance — they often just … don’t show up.
I’m sure that isn’t what happened here, though. Instead, what happens is sometimes folks new to startups can miss how much more dynamic start-ups are than public companies or bigger enterprises. Or at least, have less experience working with the type of financial model we use as start-ups. And so they may be overwhelmed by how many variables there are in a monthly burn rate plan, e.g.,:
How do the current cash balance and runway impact our assumptions around next month’s spend?
Do changes in the pipeline impact our revenue projections and thus burn rate?
Are there seasonal fluctuations in spend?
Should we account for any potential variances in sales cycles?
Or they might find themselves overwhelmed with the amount of data involved in building an accurate forecast, especially if they’re used to dealing with larger-scale financial models where these nuances aren’t as pronounced.
Whatever the reason, the fact remains that missing budget by nearly $1M each month indicates a fundamental issue with either forecasting accuracy or process reliability. Either way, it needs to be addressed ASAP.
Here’s my advice:
First, push back politely but firmly on the numbers. Ask them to explain why they think the actuals differ from the plan, line item by line item. This will help identify whether the problem lies in bad data, wrong assumptions, or something else entirely.

First, ask yourself — if you were to quit right now, would they still be able to make it without you?

If no, well … that’s not OK.

And second, let me share how I dealt with this exact same issue:

I had our VP Finance do all the forecasting and burn rate planning herself for her first few months on the job.
Then we hired an outside CFO later who was polished (as your guy is) and did everything perfectly, except he didn’t really know anything about the business or product.
We got great monthly cash flow forecasts from him, but every single month we’d miss our burn plan by $200k-$300k because he couldn’t understand why it wasn’t working out like his models said.

So after 12+ months, I realized even though we had accurate cash projections, we weren’t actually doing what needed to get done to hit those numbers. So I asked myself: If I quit today, could anyone else do my job? No one could.

Maybe. But not if you don’t understand outbound first.

The “Let’s Get Going” Camp
:
Outbound is hard, and it takes months to learn, iterate, and scale. Why wait for perfection when AI can start generating pipeline immediately? This camp argues that even mediocre AI outreach beats no outreach at all.
The “Master It First” Camp
:
AI SDRs amplify bad processes faster than they amplify good ones. You need to master outbound with humans before scaling with AI. Here’s why:
Human Outbound Teaches You What Works (and What Doesn’t)
When you run outbound campaigns manually, you get immediate feedback on messaging, timing, personalization, and response rates. You see which subject lines convert. Which pain points resonate. Who responds fastest. What time zones work best. A six-month manual experiment teaches you exactly how prospecting works for your specific buyer persona.
That institutional knowledge becomes critical when implementing AI agents. If you haven’t figured out what a great email looks like or where to find decision-makers, your AI will be guessing—and making costly mistakes.
AI Is Only as Good As Your Training Data
Think about it: your AI agent learns from everything you feed it.

Dear SaaStr: How Can I Keep Angry Customers Happy?
Angry customers are often … your best leads.
Even if they don’t think so right now.  Even if it seems like you’ve lost them forever, or at least for this year and beyond.
I know a few things:
First,
no customer is 100% happy
. Not really. They may be fairly satisfied (and that’s great), but no one is ever 100% happy with everything in B2B. And second, unhappy customers will buy again from you — if you fix the issues and problems.
So when a customer says No Way We’ll Ever Buy From You Again — well —
They’re Wrong
. At least, not always. Maybe not even most of the time.
What should you do? Here are 5 tactics to save an angry customer:
1/ Fix The Problem Now. If It’s Truly Your Fault. If it was your fault, just go out and solve the problem — quickly and efficiently. That usually works. More on how here:
The Top 10 Ways To Increase Customer Satisfaction | SaaStr
It takes some work, but if you fix their issue fast, you can win back many angry customers.
2/ Just Get On A Jet. Go Meet Them In Person. This almost never fails
. Anger fades when folks meet face-to-face. Especially after a bad experience online. Even today, even as we Zoom more than ever before. Go visit them. Do whatever it takes. Go get on a jet.
If you have a sales team, make sure everyone knows there’s a premium on saving an account. Put a commission check into anyone who saves a key customer.
3/ Give ‘Em a Break. Or Two. Yes, anger does fade. Don’t take it personally, and maybe just give them another shot, or two. Even if it’s just goodwill.
This doesn’t mean doing nothing. But sometimes, you gotta just let it go. Let it all go. Sometimes, the best thing you can do is just give someone a break, and let it go.
More
here
.
4/ Have A VP Of CS Who Knows How To Save Accounts. This works 80%+ of the time
. Having someone whose job it is to keep accounts that complain and leave … makes magic happen. Find a way. Because every single customer complains. Some just say “No” at first. A good VP of CS keeps these ones, in general. More
here
.
5/ Make Sure No One Else Leaves Either
. If your bigger competitors aren’t closing new logos, then why would any of your existing customers want to switch over? If they see you growing faster than the competition, and you are ahead, they won’t need to switch. They’ll stay, especially if they trust you. As CEO, your #1 job is to grow revenue
. Secondarily, your job is to close competitive deals. Thirdly, you manage your NPS and churn. And finally, you create a company where everyone wants to work — and stays. That creates a lot of loyalty. So if your biggest competitor isn’t winning big deals … it’s easier to retain those big customers.
And one bonus idea …
6/ Offer To Help Them Compete Better Against You
. This can work very well too! If they are going to compete against you anyway, maybe offer to help them do better. There’s only so much you can do, but sometimes offering to help them sell against you can make things less adversarial. More
here
.

. This can be earlier if you’re selling into a regulated industry or higher ACV segment. If you just want to sell over Zoom today, you may not care so much here. But if you’re looking to build something bigger, you’ll see this too.

Dear SaaStr: Is it bad to leave a struggling startup?
I don’t think so.
If you are going to stay at a struggling start-up for too long, and/or without any real ownership (equity) … then it may be OK if that’s what you want. But otherwise …
No. It’s not “bad”.
It can take startups years to get from $1m ARR to $10m+ ARR. Sometimes even longer. And sometimes … never. Even with amazing VCs and incredible teams.
You’ve got to commit to something, though.
A mediocre job isn’t worth staying somewhere you hate, or where there is no upside left for you. Just move on.
But if you truly believe — you can make a difference. If you really see the light. Then stick around as long as you can bear it. More often than not, you’ll look back later and wish you had stayed just another year.
Even if they raise another round next quarter, and things seem better … you might look back later and wish you’d stuck around. At least until your equity was fully vested.
And importantly, it’s much easier to find a new role when you already know folks in the industry. Stay where you have leverage, especially in sales, marketing, success, etc. Wherever you can keep your options open, do that.

P.S. Don’t let anyone guilt trip you into staying somewhere that doesn’t serve you well.
